source_refs.note: Book p. 186-189: 10.3 Further Application of Basic Identities, Examples 5-10 (no prose in print; Example 10 ends above Exercise 10.2)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book gives no explanation under this heading; it goes straight to six worked examples. Each example uses the identities proved in 10.1.2 (the sum and difference formulas) together with \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\) and the allied-angle rules of 10.2. Keep these at hand:
\[\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\cos(\alpha \pm \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta \mp \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\tan(\alpha \pm \beta) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \mp \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\]
\[\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\]
In \(\pm\) and \(\mp\) read the upper signs together and the lower signs together. Notice that in the cosine formula the sign in the middle is the opposite of the sign in the angle.

blocks.title: Example 5
steps:
Given: the product \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\sin(\alpha - \beta)\).
To prove: it equals \(\sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\beta\) (i), and also \(\cos^{2}\beta - \cos^{2}\alpha\) (ii).
Method: start from the L.H.S., expand both factors with the sum and difference formulas, multiply, then use \(\cos^{2}\theta = 1 - \sin^{2}\theta\) so that only sines remain.

Step 1: Expand both factors
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \sin(\alpha + \beta)\sin(\alpha - \beta)\]
\[= (\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\]
\[\times(\sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\]
Why: \(\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta\). The two brackets differ only in the middle sign.

Step 2: Multiply as \((x + y)(x - y) = x^{2} - y^{2}\)
\[= \sin^{2}\alpha\cos^{2}\beta - \cos^{2}\alpha\sin^{2}\beta\]
Why: with \(x = \sin\alpha\cos\beta\) and \(y = \cos\alpha\sin\beta\) the product is a difference of squares, so the cross terms cancel.

Step 3: Write the cosines in terms of sines
\[= \sin^{2}\alpha(1 - \sin^{2}\beta) - (1 - \sin^{2}\alpha)\sin^{2}\beta\]
\[= \sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha\sin^{2}\beta\]
\[\quad - \sin^{2}\beta + \sin^{2}\alpha\sin^{2}\beta\]
\[= \sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\beta \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: \(\cos^{2}\theta = 1 - \sin^{2}\theta\). The result (i) has only sines, so we replace each cosine; the two terms \(\sin^{2}\alpha\sin^{2}\beta\) then cancel.

Step 4: Change result (i) into cosines
\[= (1 - \cos^{2}\alpha) - (1 - \cos^{2}\beta)\]
\[= 1 - \cos^{2}\alpha - 1 + \cos^{2}\beta\]
\[= \cos^{2}\beta - \cos^{2}\alpha \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: \(\sin^{2}\theta = 1 - \cos^{2}\theta\); the 1s cancel. Watch the order: \(\cos^{2}\beta\) comes first.

Check:
Take \(\alpha = 60^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 30^{\circ}\): L.H.S. \(= \sin 90^{\circ}\sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\).
(i): \(\sin^{2}60^{\circ} - \sin^{2}30^{\circ} = \frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\).
(ii): \(\cos^{2}30^{\circ} - \cos^{2}60^{\circ} = \frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\). All three agree.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Remember this result as a ready-made identity: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\beta\). The same steps give the companion result \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\beta\) (try it as practice).

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Without using tables, find the values of all trigonometric functions of \(105^{\circ}\).
steps:
Given: the angle \(105^{\circ}\), which is not in the table of special angles.
To find: \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\), \(\cot\), \(\operatorname{cosec}\) and \(\sec\) of \(105^{\circ}\).
Method: write \(105^{\circ} = 60^{\circ} + 45^{\circ}\), two angles whose ratios we know exactly, and use the sum formulas. The other three functions are reciprocals.

Step 1: \(\sin 105^{\circ}\)
\[\sin 105^{\circ} = \sin(60^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= \sin 60^{\circ}\cos 45^{\circ} + \cos 60^{\circ}\sin 45^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\) with \(\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Step 2: \(\cos 105^{\circ}\)
\[\cos 105^{\circ} = \cos(60^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= \cos 60^{\circ}\cos 45^{\circ} - \sin 60^{\circ}\sin 45^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\). The value is negative because \(105^{\circ}\) is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative.

Step 3: \(\tan 105^{\circ}\)
\[\tan 105^{\circ} = \dfrac{\tan 60^{\circ} + \tan 45^{\circ}}{1 - \tan 60^{\circ}\tan 45^{\circ}}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{1-\sqrt{3}\cdot 1} = \dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\]
Why: \(\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\), \(\tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}\), \(\tan 45^{\circ} = 1\). (Dividing step 1 by step 2 gives the same value.)

Step 4: \(\cot 105^{\circ}\)
\[\cot 105^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\tan 105^{\circ}} = \dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}}\]
The book prints \(\cot 105^{\circ} = \frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\); the denominator should be \(1+\sqrt{3}\) (see the Book correction below).
Why: cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, so we turn the fraction of step 3 upside down.

Step 5: \(\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ}\)
\[\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sin 105^{\circ}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}+1}\]
The book prints \(\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}\), which is the value of \(\sin 105^{\circ}\), not its reciprocal (see the Book correction below).
Why: cosecant is the reciprocal of sine; invert the fraction of step 1.

Step 6: \(\sec 105^{\circ}\)
\[\sec 105^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\cos 105^{\circ}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\]
Why: secant is the reciprocal of cosine; invert the fraction of step 2.

Check:
\[\sin^{2}105^{\circ} + \cos^{2}105^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2} + (1-\sqrt{3})^{2}}{8}\]
\[= \dfrac{(4+2\sqrt{3}) + (4-2\sqrt{3})}{8} = 1\]
Signs: in quadrant II only \(\sin\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}\) are positive; our \(\cos\), \(\tan\), \(\cot\), \(\sec\) are all negative because \(1-\sqrt{3} < 0\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In Example 6 the book prints two wrong reciprocal values:
1. \(\cot 105^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 105^{\circ}} = \frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\) (which would equal 1). Correct: \(\cot 105^{\circ} = \frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3} - 2\).
2. \(\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 105^{\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}\) (this is \(\sin 105^{\circ}\) itself). Correct: \(\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}+1} = \sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The answers can be simplified by rationalizing (multiplying top and bottom by a suitable expression):
\(\sin 105^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}\), \(\cos 105^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{6}}{4}\), \(\tan 105^{\circ} = -(2+\sqrt{3})\), \(\cot 105^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}-2\), \(\operatorname{cosec} 105^{\circ} = \sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}\), \(\sec 105^{\circ} = -(\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2})\).
For example, \(\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\times\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}} = \frac{4+2\sqrt{3}}{-2} = -(2+\sqrt{3})\). Either form is accepted unless the question asks for a simplified answer.

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: \(\frac{\cos 11^{\circ} + \sin 11^{\circ}}{\cos 11^{\circ} - \sin 11^{\circ}}\) and \(\tan 56^{\circ}\).
To prove: they are equal.
Method: notice that \(56^{\circ} = 45^{\circ} + 11^{\circ}\). Start from the R.H.S., expand with the \(\tan(\alpha + \beta)\) formula, use \(\tan 45^{\circ} = 1\), then write \(\tan 11^{\circ} = \frac{\sin 11^{\circ}}{\cos 11^{\circ}}\).

Step 1: Expand the R.H.S.
\[\text{R.H.S.} = \tan 56^{\circ} = \tan(45^{\circ} + 11^{\circ})\]
\[= \dfrac{\tan 45^{\circ} + \tan 11^{\circ}}{1 - \tan 45^{\circ}\tan 11^{\circ}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 + \tan 11^{\circ}}{1 - \tan 11^{\circ}}\]
Why: \(45^{\circ}\) is the angle whose tangent is 1, so it makes the formula very simple.

Step 2: Change tangent into sine and cosine
\[= \dfrac{1 + \frac{\sin 11^{\circ}}{\cos 11^{\circ}}}{1 - \frac{\sin 11^{\circ}}{\cos 11^{\circ}}}\]
\[= \dfrac{\cos 11^{\circ} + \sin 11^{\circ}}{\cos 11^{\circ} - \sin 11^{\circ}} = \text{L.H.S.}\]
Why: the L.H.S. has sines and cosines. Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by \(\cos 11^{\circ}\) clears the small fractions.

Check:
With a calculator: \(\cos 11^{\circ} \approx 0.9816\), \(\sin 11^{\circ} \approx 0.1908\), so the L.H.S. \(\approx \frac{1.1724}{0.7908} \approx 1.4826\), and \(\tan 56^{\circ} \approx 1.4826\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The pattern \(\frac{\cos x + \sin x}{\cos x - \sin x} = \frac{1 + \tan x}{1 - \tan x} = \tan(45^{\circ} + x)\) appears often. In the same way \(\frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x + \sin x} = \tan(45^{\circ} - x)\).

blocks.title: Example 8
blocks.problem: If \(\cos\alpha = -\frac{7}{25}\), \(\tan\beta = \frac{12}{5}\), the terminal side of the angle of measure \(\alpha\) is in the II quadrant and that of \(\beta\) is in the III quadrant, find the values of: (i) \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\) (ii) \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\). In which quadrant does the terminal side of the angle of measure \((\alpha + \beta)\) lie?
steps:
Given: \(\cos\alpha = -\frac{7}{25}\) with \(\alpha\) in quadrant II; \(\tan\beta = \frac{12}{5}\) with \(\beta\) in quadrant III.
To find: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\), \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\) and the quadrant of \(\alpha + \beta\).
Method: the sum formulas need \(\sin\alpha\), \(\cos\alpha\), \(\sin\beta\), \(\cos\beta\). Find the missing ones with the Pythagorean identities, and fix every sign from the quadrant.

Step 1: Find \(\sin\alpha\)
\[\sin\alpha = \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\alpha}\]
\[= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(-\dfrac{7}{25}\right)^{2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{576}{625}}\]
\[= \pm\dfrac{24}{25}\]
The terminal side of \(\alpha\) is in quadrant II, where \(\sin\alpha\) is positive. The book then prints 'So \(\sin\alpha = -\frac{24}{25}\)'; the sign should be plus (see the Book correction below).
\[\sin\alpha = \dfrac{24}{25}\]
Why: from \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha = 1\); \(625 - 49 = 576 = 24^{2}\). The square root gives two signs and the quadrant chooses one.

Step 2: Find \(\sec\beta\) and \(\cos\beta\)
\[\sec\beta = \pm\sqrt{1 + \tan^{2}\beta} = \pm\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right)^{2}}\]
\[= \pm\dfrac{13}{5}\]
In quadrant III \(\sec\beta\) is negative:
\[\sec\beta = -\dfrac{13}{5}, \quad \cos\beta = -\dfrac{5}{13}\]
Why: \(1 + \tan^{2}\beta = \sec^{2}\beta\) connects the given \(\tan\beta\) with \(\sec\beta\); \(25 + 144 = 169 = 13^{2}\). Cosine is the reciprocal of secant.

Step 3: Find \(\sin\beta\)
\[\sin\beta = \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\beta} = \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{25}{169}}\]
\[= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{144}{169}} = \pm\dfrac{12}{13}\]
In quadrant III \(\sin\beta\) is negative: \(\sin\beta = -\frac{12}{13}\).
Why: same identity as step 1. Quick check: \(\frac{\sin\beta}{\cos\beta} = \frac{-12/13}{-5/13} = \frac{12}{5} = \tan\beta\).

Step 4: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\)
\[\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[= \dfrac{24}{25}\left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right) + \left(-\dfrac{7}{25}\right)\left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{-120 + 84}{325} = -\dfrac{36}{325}\]
Why: the sum formula for sine; \(25 \times 13 = 325\). A negative times a negative is positive, so the second term is \(+\frac{84}{325}\).

Step 5: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\)
\[\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[= \left(-\dfrac{7}{25}\right)\left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right) - \dfrac{24}{25}\left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{35 + 288}{325} = \dfrac{323}{325}\]
Why: the sum formula for cosine; subtracting a negative product adds it.

Step 6: Quadrant of \(\alpha + \beta\)
\(\sin(\alpha + \beta) < 0\) and \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) > 0\), so the terminal arm of \(\alpha + \beta\) is in quadrant IV.
Why: quadrant IV is the only quadrant where cosine is positive and sine is negative.

Check:
\[\left(-\dfrac{36}{325}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{323}{325}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1296 + 104329}{105625} = 1\]
So the two answers are consistent with \(\sin^{2} + \cos^{2} = 1\).
blocks.answer: (i) \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = -\frac{36}{325}\) (ii) \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{323}{325}\); the terminal side of \(\alpha + \beta\) lies in quadrant IV.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 8 the book says that \(\sin\alpha\) is positive in quadrant II and then prints 'So \(\sin\alpha = -\frac{24}{25}\)'. The correct value is \(\sin\alpha = +\frac{24}{25}\); the book's own later working uses \(\frac{24}{25}\), so its final answers are right.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: If \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are the angles of \(\Delta ABC\), prove that: (i) \(\tan\alpha + \tan\beta + \tan\gamma = \tan\alpha\tan\beta\tan\gamma\) (ii) \(\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\tan\frac{\beta}{2} + \tan\frac{\beta}{2}\tan\frac{\gamma}{2} + \tan\frac{\gamma}{2}\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = 1\)
steps:
Given: \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are the angles of a triangle, so \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^{\circ}\).
To prove: the two tangent results (i) and (ii).
Method: write the sum of two angles in terms of the third, take \(\tan\) of both sides, expand with \(\tan(\alpha + \beta)\) and the allied-angle rules, then cross-multiply.

Step 1 (i): Express \(\alpha + \beta\) through \(\gamma\)
\[\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^{\circ}\]
\[\alpha + \beta = 180^{\circ} - \gamma\]
\[\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \tan(180^{\circ} - \gamma)\]
Why: equal angles have equal tangents. This links all three angles in one equation.

Step 2 (i): Expand both sides
\[\dfrac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = -\tan\gamma\]
Why: left side by the sum formula; right side by the allied-angle rule \(\tan(180^{\circ} - \gamma) = -\tan\gamma\) (\(180^{\circ}\) is an even multiple of \(90^{\circ}\), so tan stays tan, and \(180^{\circ} - \gamma\) is in quadrant II where tan is negative).

Step 3 (i): Cross-multiply and rearrange
\[\tan\alpha + \tan\beta = -\tan\gamma + \tan\alpha\tan\beta\tan\gamma\]
\[\tan\alpha + \tan\beta + \tan\gamma = \tan\alpha\tan\beta\tan\gamma\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta\), then add \(\tan\gamma\) to both sides.

Step 4 (ii): Use half angles
\[\dfrac{\alpha}{2} + \dfrac{\beta}{2} + \dfrac{\gamma}{2} = 90^{\circ}\]
\[\dfrac{\alpha}{2} + \dfrac{\beta}{2} = 90^{\circ} - \dfrac{\gamma}{2}\]
\[\tan\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2} + \dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = \tan\left(90^{\circ} - \dfrac{\gamma}{2}\right)\]
Why: the result (ii) contains half angles, so we divide the angle sum by 2.

Step 5 (ii): Expand both sides
\[\dfrac{\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} + \tan\frac{\beta}{2}}{1 - \tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\tan\frac{\beta}{2}} = \cot\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{\gamma}{2}}\]
Why: \(\tan(90^{\circ} - \theta) = \cot\theta\) (\(90^{\circ}\) is an odd multiple of \(90^{\circ}\), so tan changes to its co-ratio cot; quadrant I, positive).

Step 6 (ii): Cross-multiply and rearrange
\[\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\tan\dfrac{\gamma}{2} + \tan\dfrac{\beta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\]
\[= 1 - \tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\tan\dfrac{\beta}{2}\]
Moving the last term to the left:
\[\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\tan\dfrac{\beta}{2} + \tan\dfrac{\beta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\]
\[+ \tan\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = 1\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(\tan\frac{\gamma}{2}\) and by the denominator, then collect all products on one side.

Check:
Equilateral triangle, \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 60^{\circ}\): (i) \(3\sqrt{3} = (\sqrt{3})^{3} = 3\sqrt{3}\). (ii) \(\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so the sum is \(3\times\frac{1}{3} = 1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Result (i) needs all three tangents to exist, so it is for a triangle with no right angle (\(\tan 90^{\circ}\) is undefined). Result (ii) holds for every triangle, because each half angle is less than \(90^{\circ}\).

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: Express \(3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta\) in the form \(r\sin(\theta + \phi)\), where the terminal side of the angle of measure \(\phi\) is in quadrant I.
steps:
Given: the expression \(3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta\).
To find: \(r\) and \(\phi\) (with \(\phi\) in quadrant I) such that \(3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = r\sin(\theta + \phi)\).
Method: expand \(r\sin(\theta + \phi) = r\cos\phi\sin\theta + r\sin\phi\cos\theta\) and match coefficients: \(r\cos\phi = 3\), \(r\sin\phi = 4\).

Step 1: Set up the two equations
\[3 = r\cos\phi \quad \text{(i)}\]
\[4 = r\sin\phi \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: the coefficient of \(\sin\theta\) is \(r\cos\phi\) and the coefficient of \(\cos\theta\) is \(r\sin\phi\).

Step 2: Square and add (i) and (ii) to get \(r\)
\[3^{2} + 4^{2} = r^{2}\cos^{2}\phi + r^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\]
\[9 + 16 = r^{2}(\cos^{2}\phi + \sin^{2}\phi)\]
\[25 = r^{2} \Rightarrow r = 5\]
Why: squaring and adding removes \(\phi\) because \(\cos^{2}\phi + \sin^{2}\phi = 1\). We take \(r > 0\).

Step 3: Divide (ii) by (i) to get \(\phi\)
\[\dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{r\sin\phi}{r\cos\phi} = \tan\phi\]
\[\phi = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3}\]
Why: dividing removes \(r\). Since \(\sin\phi\) and \(\cos\phi\) are both positive, \(\phi\) is in quadrant I as required (about \(53.13^{\circ}\)).

Step 4: Write the expression in the required form
\[3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = r\cos\phi\sin\theta + r\sin\phi\cos\theta\]
\[= r(\sin\theta\cos\phi + \cos\theta\sin\phi)\]
\[= r\sin(\theta + \phi)\]
Why: replace 3 and 4 by (i) and (ii), take \(r\) common, and recognise the sum formula for sine.

Check:
\(\cos\phi = \frac{3}{5}\), \(\sin\phi = \frac{4}{5}\), so \(5\sin(\theta + \phi) = 5\left(\frac{3}{5}\sin\theta + \frac{4}{5}\cos\theta\right) = 3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
General rule: \(a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = r\sin(\theta + \phi)\) with \(r = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}\) and \(\tan\phi = \frac{b}{a}\).
For a difference, \(a\sin\theta - b\cos\theta = r\sin(\theta - \phi)\) with the same \(r\) and \(\phi\) (expand \(r\sin(\theta - \phi)\) to see why). You will use this in Exercise 10.2, Question 15.
Because \(-1 \le \sin(\theta + \phi) \le 1\), the greatest value of \(3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta\) is 5 and the least is \(-5\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. To find exact ratios of angles such as \(105^{\circ}\), \(15^{\circ}\), \(75^{\circ}\), write them as sums or differences of \(30^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}, 60^{\circ}\).
2. \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\beta = \cos^{2}\beta - \cos^{2}\alpha\).
3. \(\frac{1 + \tan x}{1 - \tan x} = \tan(45^{\circ} + x)\).
4. When one ratio and the quadrant are given, find the other ratios with \(\sin^{2} + \cos^{2} = 1\) or \(1 + \tan^{2} = \sec^{2}\), and choose each sign from the quadrant.
5. In a triangle \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^{\circ}\); write one angle in terms of the others and take tan.
6. \(a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = r\sin(\theta + \phi)\), \(r = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\), \(\tan\phi = \frac{b}{a}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\sin(60^{\circ} + 45^{\circ}) = \sin 60^{\circ} + \sin 45^{\circ}\). Sine does not distribute over addition; use the formula.
2. Using the wrong middle sign in \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\): it is minus.
3. Forgetting the quadrant when taking a square root: \(\pm\) must be decided, not dropped.
4. Inverting only part of a fraction when finding \(\cot\), \(\operatorname{cosec}\), \(\sec\): turn the whole fraction upside down.
5. In \(a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta\), taking \(\tan\phi = \frac{a}{b}\) instead of \(\frac{b}{a}\).
